newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish premier and challenger clash on N. Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Irish premier and challenger clash on N. Ireland.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, risking the wrath of nationalist voters in Friday's election, said on Wednesday that Northern Ireland's pro-British Unionists were Irish people who needed befriending.

He made his remarks in an hour-long television debate with his challenger Bertie Ahern, whose Fianna Fail party says it is the authentic voice of Irish republicans who want to reunite the British province under Dublin's rule.

His remark seemed certain to infuriate Unionists, Protestants who see themselves and Northern Ireland as a British enclave surrounded by a hostile Catholic Ireland whose constitutution lays claim to the province.

It was too early to say what effect Bruton's words might have on voters. Opionion polls show Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats consistently ahead but by too narrow a margin to ensure an overall victory.

Bruton, head of a centre-left coalition, and Ahern, whose party is allied with the Progressive Democrats in a centre-right bloc, traded well-worn arguments about taxation, unemployment and crime before tackling Northern Ireland.

Ahern accused Bruton of allowing an Anglo-Irish peace initiative on Northern Ireland to slow to a standstill during his 2-1/2-year tenure. "The peace process has stalled under this government," he said.

Bruton, often dubbed "Unionist John" by his critics for seeking to safeguard the interests of both Northern Ireland's Protestant majority and Catholic minority, said that bridges had to be built between the two communities to make peace.
"I believe the Unionists are Irish people and the Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) has to befriend them," Bruton said. "Our job is to build bridges and to be fair to both sides."
He was responding to Ahern, who said his coalition would "stand up" for the rights of the Catholic minority in Northern Ireland against both the British government and Unionists.
"The (Irish) nationalist community feels that they have been alientated. They want to see someone stand up for them. They want to see somebody who understands their problems," he said.
"The Irish Taoseach (prime minister) has a special position. It is to understand the 40 percent (Catholic minority)," Ahern countered.

It was only the second time in a three-week campaign that Northern Ireland had surfaced as a contentious issue and both leaders agreed that the top priority of the next government would have to be to bring about Northern Ireland peace.

Ahern served under former prime minister Albert Reynolds, who helped broker a ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) which launched the current peace process. The latest round of talks started in Belfast on Wednesday.
He accused Bruton of allowing the opportunity of the ceasefire to slip away while Britain demanded that the IRA agree to disarm before giving its political wing, Sinn Fein, a seat at the peace talks.

Bruton denied the charge and pointed out that the talks, from which Sinn Fein is excluded until there is a permanent IRA ceasefire, began in Belfast while he was prime minister in June last year after a bitter wrangle with Britain.
